final_proof:
Let f be the continuous 2π-periodic function whose restriction to [−π,π] is f(x)=x². (The periodic extension is continuous because f(−π)=f(π)=π².) We first compute its Fourier coefficients, using the convention

a₀=(1/π)∫_{−π}^{π}f(x) dx,   aₙ=(1/π)∫_{−π}^{π}f(x)cos(nx) dx,   bₙ=(1/π)∫_{−π}^{π}f(x)sin(nx) dx.

Since f is even, bₙ=0 for every n≥1, and

a₀=(2/π)∫₀^π x² dx=2π²/3.

For n≥1, two integrations by parts give

∫₀^π x²cos(nx) dx=[x²sin(nx)/n+2x cos(nx)/n²−2sin(nx)/n³]₀^π=2π(−1)ⁿ/n².

Consequently,

aₙ=(2/π)∫₀^π x²cos(nx) dx=4(−1)ⁿ/n².   (1)

We now justify fully that these coefficients recover f. This is needed rather than merely assuming convergence of the Fourier series. The series ∑ₙ₌₁^∞1/n² converges: for n≥2, 1/n²≤1/(n(n−1))=1/(n−1)−1/n. Hence the series

g(x)=π²/3+4∑ₙ₌₁^∞ (−1)ⁿcos(nx)/n²   (2)

converges uniformly on ℝ by the Weierstrass M-test. Thus g is continuous and 2π-periodic, and its Fourier coefficients may be computed term by term. By the elementary orthogonality relations for sines and cosines, they are precisely the coefficients in (1), together with a₀=2π²/3 and bₙ=0. Therefore h=f−g is a continuous 2π-periodic function all of whose Fourier coefficients vanish.

For completeness, we prove that this forces h=0. For N≥0 define the Fejér kernel

K_N(t)=1+2∑ₙ₌₁^N(1−n/(N+1))cos(nt)=1/(N+1)·(sin((N+1)t/2)/sin(t/2))²,

where the value at multiples of 2π is understood by continuity. The second expression shows that K_N≥0, while the first shows that ∫_{−π}^{π}K_N(t)dt=2π. The Nth Fejér mean of the Fourier series of h is

σ_N(h;x)=(1/(2π))∫_{−π}^{π}h(x−t)K_N(t)dt.   (3)

Indeed, expanding the finite sum defining K_N and using the angle-addition formulas gives exactly the usual weighted sum of the Fourier coefficients of h. Since every one of those coefficients is zero, (3) equals zero for every N and x.

On the other hand, σ_N(h;·) converges uniformly to h. To see this directly, let ε>0. Uniform continuity of the periodic function h gives a δ∈(0,π) such that |h(x−t)−h(x)|<ε whenever |t|<δ, uniformly in x. If M=max|h|, then for δ≤|t|≤π we have

K_N(t)≤1/((N+1)sin²(δ/2)).

Using K_N≥0 and its integral, we therefore obtain

|σ_N(h;x)−h(x)|≤ε+(1/(2π))·2M·2π/((N+1)sin²(δ/2)),

uniformly in x. The second term tends to zero. Thus σ_N(h;x)→h(x) uniformly. Since every σ_N(h;x) is zero, h(x)=0 for all x. It follows that f=g everywhere.

Finally, put x=π in (2). Since cos(nπ)=(−1)ⁿ, we get

π²=π²/3+4∑ₙ₌₁^∞1/n².

Rearranging yields

∑ₙ₌₁^∞1/n²=π²/6.

By the definition ζ(2)=∑ₙ₌₁^∞n⁻², this is ζ(2)=π²/6, as claimed.
